records.decision_text: I accepted the only apartment I could afford because the other available places were outside my budget; I had no realistic alternative.
I wanted to accept the uncertain overseas role, but my family persuaded me to stay in my current position, so I chose not to go.
I felt nervous and excited about moving, but I listed the costs, compared three-year budgets, and chose the option with the stronger financial plan.

I usually say I welcome uncertainty and want ambitious projects, but I also avoid uncertain choices whenever I can. For this project I selected the predictable assignment because I did not want to risk disrupting my routine.

I moved to a smaller town for a role with uncertain pay because it offered the kind of work I want long term. I decided after comparing the relocation costs and a three-year budget, while considering how the change would affect my partner.
I always make bold choices, and I chose to leave my predictable contract for a role where the results depend on a new product launch.

For most of the spring I compared commute routes, reviewed neighborhood maps, asked friends about local services, and kept notes on what mattered to me. I also spent several weekends visiting open houses. My calendar was crowded with work and errands, and I postponed the choice while gathering more information. I spoke with several people about their experiences and made a list of possible drawbacks. In the end, the one factor that settled it was that the lease gave me a lower rent for the next two years, which fit the savings goal I had set for myself. I signed after reviewing the final numbers.
